Q116182097.summary: Seen through a covering of rock crystal, a tiny gold plaque engraved in niello shows Christ on the cross, bearded, with a cross-nimbus and dressed in the long sleeveless colobium. At the ends of the arms stand the Virgin, raising her hand in grief, and John the Evangelist with his Gospel; above are the sun and moon and the letters naming Jesus Christ, and across the arms runs Christ's word from the cross, 'Behold your son… behold your mother.' This little reliquary of the True Cross, sent by a pope to a queen, links the earliest Eastern images of the Crucifixion with the conversion of the Lombards.
facts: According to tradition Pope Gregory the Great gave it in 603 to Queen Theodelinda for the baptism of her son Adaloald, the future Lombard king.
It is a staurotheke, made to hold a fragment of the wood of the Cross inserted in Christ's tunic; the relic itself is now lost.
Pope Paul VI wore the cross on his pilgrimage to the Holy Land in January 1964.
Q116182097.notes: Sources differ on origin: Italian Wikipedia calls the gold plaque 'Syrian art of the 6th century' and also suggests manufacture in Rome; German Wikipedia says possibly made in Syria and reworked in Rome. The rock-crystal cover is not original (documented by 1713), and the gold of the reverse may be a later (possibly Carolingian) remaking. 603 is the date of the gift, not necessarily of manufacture.

Q140797834.summary: Painted on the wall of the south transept of Bonn Minster, a pale cloth carries the dark, frontal face of Christ, framed by long hair falling to either side — the 'true image' that, according to medieval legend, Christ left on the veil Veronica offered him on the way to Calvary. The painting is damaged and the face has darkened, but its stark frontality still conveys the devotional force of the Vera Icon, an image pilgrims sought in Rome and copied throughout late-medieval Europe.
Q140797834.scripture: Luke 23:26–31 (theme: the way to Calvary; the Veronica episode is not in the Gospels)
facts: The Veronica legend is not found in the Gospels; devotion to the Roman relic grew strongly from the 13th century, encouraged in part by Pope Innocent III, and the name 'Veronica' has been linked to the phrase vera icon, 'true image'.
Bonn Minster was largely rebuilt in late Romanesque and early Gothic style; its transept ends in polygonal conchs, in one of which this painting is found.
Q140797834.notes: The date c. 1320 comes from Wikidata (sourced to Bildindex der Kunst und Architektur, object 0002190240), which could not be consulted directly (bot-protected); treat as approximate. Placement from the Commons description (south conch, left of the altar of St John / Baptism of Christ).

cur:catacombs-tarragona-bethesda.summary: Set into the cathedral façade, the front shows five scenes from left to right: the healing of the blind, the healing of the woman with the issue of blood, the healing of the paralytic at the pool of Bethesda – shown in two tiers – the encounter with Zacchaeus and Christ's triumphal entry into Jerusalem.
facts: The healing at the pool of Bethesda is carved in two tiers at the centre, giving the front its name.
This example is built into the façade of Tarragona cathedral above the right side door.

cur:catacombs-bargello-couple-crowned-by.summary: In the central medallion a husband and wife are crowned by a small figure of Christ above them; around them radiate panels with standing saints and their names, like the spokes of a wheel. Cut from the base of a bowl, such glasses were pressed into the mortar of catacomb tombs as markers and keepsakes.
facts: It was shown at the exhibition 'Pretiosa vitrea' in Florence in 2017–2018.
Gold glass was made by sandwiching cut gold leaf between two layers of fused glass.

Q3221346.summary: Christ, robed in white and crowned with thorns, descends the steps of Pilate's palace into a seething crowd, while below him workmen lay out the cross he is about to carry. His calm, luminous figure stands out against the dark, tumultuous mass of soldiers, priests and mourners. Doré, best known as an illustrator of the Bible and Dante, considered this immense canvas the work of his life.
facts: At about 6 by 9 metres it is the largest of Doré's religious paintings.

Completed in April 1872, it was shown for some twenty years at the Doré Gallery in London's New Bond Street, where crowds paid to see his religious canvases, before touring the United States from 1892.
Doré painted replicas as well; a slightly smaller version is in the Musée d'Arts de Nantes, and the original was bought by Strasbourg, his birthplace, in 1988.
